clue.text: A little vicar used to be high-flier (for a while)

indicators.note: Asking for a little of something means a small helping taken out of the middle of it rather than the whole thing.

parts.note: six letters running consecutively from the second letter of the first word, straight across the gap into the second

explanation.walkthrough: The bracket is the joke: the Greek boy's wax wings held him up until the sun got at them. A parish clergyman is the disguise, and none of him is wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: high-flier (for a while) → ICARUS: he soared on wings of feathers and wax until the sun melted them, so the height lasted no time at all.

clue.text: Explained: goat maybe ingredient for frying

parts.note: to clarify a point is to explain it, making it clear
a goat butts with its horns, so it is one that butts, and 'maybe' flags it as only one example of such a creature

explanation.walkthrough: The colon dresses 'Explained' up as a heading introducing the rest of the sentence, when it is really the first half of a two-part build.
explanation.definitionFit: Butter simmered until the milk solids are strained off is ghee, which takes a much higher heat in the pan without burning.

clue.text: Most intense potpourri chests will contain

indicators.note: What a thing contains is already sitting inside it, so the letters are there untouched and in order, waiting to be read off.

parts.note: seven consecutive letters beginning near the end of the first word and running on into the second

explanation.walkthrough: Potpourri and chests belong to a surface picture of a scented drawer. Neither is being defined — they are only the wrapping the letters travel in.
explanation.definitionFit: Most intense → RICHEST: of a colour, a flavour or a sound, rich means deep and concentrated, so the superlative is the most intense of them.

clue.text: Avoid narrow streets in cold-weather vehicles

parts.note: to skip a meeting is to avoid going to it
a lane is the narrowest kind of street, wide enough for a single line of traffic

explanation.walkthrough: 'Avoid narrow streets' reads as advice to a driver, and that is the whole trap: the two words are clued separately, with the hyphen in the enumeration marking the join.
explanation.definitionFit: cold-weather vehicles → SKI-PLANES: aircraft fitted with long runners in place of wheels, so they can land on snow and ice.

clue.text: Take as read: Everyman twit first and foremost; secondarily, buffoon

indicators.note: Something described as first and foremost goes to the head of the queue, so this piece opens the answer instead of sitting where the clue mentions it.

parts.note: calling someone an ass is calling them a fool, which is what a twit is

indicators.note: To come secondarily is to come in second place, and that place is counted into the word beside it: keep the letter standing there and drop the rest.

parts.note: the letter standing in position two of that word
the setter signs every one of these puzzles with that name, so when he writes it he means himself

explanation.walkthrough: The semicolon separates two instructions that read as one long insult. Everyman's own byline is a piece of the wordplay, which is a habit worth expecting in this puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: Take as read → ASSUME: to take a thing as read is to treat it as settled without checking it, which is precisely what assuming is.

clue.text: By the side of a pine

parts.note: the single letter taken straight off the clue
to pine for someone is to long for them

explanation.walkthrough: 'a pine' offers you a tree, and the tree is a noun. The clue wants the verb, and five letters is far too few for a species anyway.
explanation.definitionFit: By the side of → ALONG: the sense in 'a path along the wall', meaning beside and following it, rather than the 'come along' sense.

clue.text: Relative in cowboy hat having change of heart

indicators.note: the heart, the central letter of the hat's name, is changed for another letter

parts.note: a Stetson is the wide-brimmed hat worn by cowboys
the middle letter of the hat's name
the replacement letter

explanation.surface: A family member turns up in a cowboy hat, having changed their mind about something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Change of heart' is read literally: the heart of STETSON is its middle T, which becomes P.
explanation.definitionFit: A stepson is a family connection by marriage, the son of one's spouse, so he counts as a relative.

clue.text: Rude intent might — possibly — give you this?

definitions.text: Rude intent might — possibly — give you this?

indicators.note: Possibly says the letters could come out any number of ways, which is licence to rearrange them rather than read them as they stand.

parts.note: fifteen letters of fodder, exactly the count the enumeration asks for

explanation.walkthrough: The dashes make 'possibly' look like an aside from the setter. Read straight, the sentence describes a state of mind; read again, its first three words are the raw material for it.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue defines: someone whose intent is rude has exactly this, a habit of finding the smutty reading in anything said to them.

clue.text: Much water wanting vigorous aeration, carbon thrice

indicators.note: Anything done vigorously is done hard enough to shake things out of their places, so the letters beside the word will not stay where they were put.

parts.note: eight letters of fodder, handed over whole
C is the chemical symbol for carbon, and it is wanted three times over

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a fish tank in need of a pump. Counting eleven letters of fodder against the (6,5) enumeration is what confirms the shuffle before any answer suggests itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Much water → ARCTIC OCEAN: an ocean is the largest body of water there is, and this is the one that sits on top of the globe.

clue.text: Small worm, exhausted, clenching — first to crawl?

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels

indicators.note: the outer letters grip the next piece between them
an exhausted worm has had its insides used up, leaving only its outer letters

parts.note: the word whose outer letters are kept
I is the Roman numeral one, and one is first

explanation.surface: A small, worn-out worm grips something as it begins to crawl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First' gives I by way of one, the Roman numeral. The question mark warns that crawl is not creeping but a swimming stroke.
explanation.definitionFit: The crawl is the front swimming stroke, so to crawl in water is to move through it with that stroke.

clue.text: Tower: look up

indicators.note: This is a down entry, so a piece told to go up is written from the bottom of the grid towards the top — backwards, in other words.

parts.note: a quick look is a peek, and here it is written climbing the grid instead of descending it

explanation.walkthrough: The colon does all the misdirection. 'Tower: look up' reads as an instruction to raise your eyes, when the second half is simply a word to be turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: Tower → KEEP: the keep is the great central tower of a castle, the stronghold defenders fall back to when the outer walls are lost.

clue.text: Ashen prisoner accepting fine, showing sign of submission

indicators.note: To accept something is to take it on, and the prisoner here takes the letter on at his front — a loose join rather than a true swallowing.

parts.note: a face drained of all its colour is described as ashen
F is the grade stamped on a pencil for fine, the harder, thinner lead
an old lag is British slang for a convict who has served plenty of time

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a convict taking his punishment on the chin. F for fine is the pencil grade, nothing to do with money, and it is the smallest of the three pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: sign of submission → WHITE FLAG: the plain pale cloth raised on a battlefield to signal surrender and ask for terms.

clue.text: Take control of waters, as dictated

indicators.note: Dictation is words spoken for somebody else to write down, so what counts is the sound of the word and not the way it is spelt.

parts.note: the world's great bodies of water are the seas, and that single sound has a second spelling in English

explanation.walkthrough: One sound, two spellings, and the naval surface — taking control of the waters — is smooth enough that the whole device is easy to walk straight past.
explanation.definitionFit: Take control of → SEIZE: to seize a ship, a town or a chance is to take hold of it suddenly and by force.

clue.text: Perhaps lick fourth of stamps: it's one that's damaged

indicators.note: Something damaged has been knocked out of shape, so the letters it names no longer sit in the order they arrived in.
Counting to the fourth of anything picks out the single item standing in position four, which here is a letter and not a stamp.

parts.note: count four letters into the word and stop there
six letters of fodder, taken exactly as they are written, apostrophe ignored

explanation.walkthrough: The colon makes the clue read as a note to self — lick the stamps — and the two halves of that phrase are doing quite different jobs, one defining and one surrendering a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Perhaps lick → MOISTEN: licking a stamp is one way of moistening it, so the definition offers an example of the action rather than a synonym for it.

clue.text: Steadily, at pool table, sinks last of seven … on … on a roll

indicators.note: Something on a roll is turning over and over, so the assembly built before it is read back the other way.

parts.note: to sink a ball on a pool table is to pot it
the closing letter of that number written out
the little word taken at face value

explanation.walkthrough: Everyman strings the sentence out with ellipses so that 'on ... on' reads as a chant from the crowd. Only the first of the two is a piece; the second belongs to the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Steadily → NON-STOP: to talk or work non-stop is to keep at it without a break, which is doing it steadily.

clue.text: Spray blue rinse all over the place

indicators.note: Things all over the place are scattered with no order to them, which is what becomes of the letters standing beside the phrase.

parts.note: nine letters of fodder, the same count the enumeration asks for

explanation.walkthrough: A blue rinse is the pale tint an old-fashioned hairdresser puts on grey hair, which is why the phrase sits so comfortably next to a spray. It is material, not description.
explanation.definitionFit: Spray → NEBULISER: the device that turns liquid medicine into a fine mist for an asthma patient to breathe in.

clue.text: Censors in Communist legislation

parts.note: a red has meant a communist ever since the colour of the revolutionary flag
laws that have passed through parliament are acts

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a headline about state control of the press, and that is the whole disguise — the two halves are separate pieces laid end to end.
explanation.definitionFit: Censors → REDACTS: to redact a document is to black out the sensitive parts before releasing it, the official word for censoring on paper.

clue.text: Disputes files

definitions.meaning: the noisy-quarrel sense, the one that rhymes with cows
soldiers drawn up in ranks and files are standing in lines, and a line of things is the other reading

explanation.walkthrough: Two words and no other wordplay, and the sly part is that the two are not even said the same way: one rhymes with cows, the other with nose.
explanation.definitionFit: Disputes gives the shouting-match sense; 'files' gives the straight-line sense, as in the ranks and files of a parade ground.

clue.text: Provençal character?

definitions.meaning: the surface offers a person from Provence; the setter is holding the word itself up for inspection, hook and all
not a personality but a written mark, the sense in which a keyboard carries a hundred of them

explanation.walkthrough: The clue is its own example: the mark being described is printed right there under the c of Provençal, and 'character' quietly trades a person for a piece of type.
explanation.definitionFit: The little hook written beneath a c to soften it to an s sound, used in French and Portuguese — and shown off in the clue's own first word.

clue.text: Receptacles for pelts

definitions.meaning: the plain sense: the things you carry water in
when rain pelts down it comes in torrents — a verb about heavy weather, not the animal skins the surface offers

explanation.walkthrough: 'Receptacles for pelts' conjures a tannery, and that is the entire misdirection: 'pelts' is what rain does, so both halves are straight definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: Receptacles are buckets in the pail sense; 'pelts' is the weather verb, since rain that pelts down is rain that buckets down.

clue.text: Monster, one I only mentioned?

definitions.meaning: the straight half — a giant out of Homer, the shepherd Odysseus blinded with a burning stake
on the page that is the pronoun, but in the mouth it is the organ this giant has exactly one of

explanation.walkthrough: The joke lives entirely in the ear: written down it is a pronoun, spoken it is an eye, and a single eye is the one thing everybody knows about the creature.
explanation.definitionFit: A one-eyed giant of Greek myth: the clue's 'one I' is that solitary eye, so the sentence describes the monster rather than building it out of letters.

clue.text: Primarily slangy expression signifying hangin'?

indicators.note: Primarily points at what comes first, so each word after it surrenders nothing but the letter it opens with.

parts.note: the four initials, read straight off the four words in the order they stand

explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe on 'hangin'' does double duty: it marks the dropped g of casual speech, and casual speech is exactly the register of the word being spelled out.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue defines: a clipped, slangy shortening of 'session', the word for an evening spent drinking or hanging about with friends.

clue.text: Tightened injury

definitions.meaning: the past tense of wind: a clock spring that has been turned tight
a cut or a gash, the noun a nurse dresses and bandages

explanation.walkthrough: Two words side by side and nothing else to go on. They share five letters and no sound at all: one rhymes with found, the other with tuned.
explanation.definitionFit: Tightened is the past tense of wind, as a spring is; injury is the gash sense — the same five letters spelling two unrelated words.

clue.text: Where Woods would use woods — or woods?

definitions.meaning: Tiger Woods is the golfer, and the place he would swing a driver is a venue with a course and a clubhouse
a wood is the club with the big rounded head, once carved from persimmon and now made of metal

explanation.walkthrough: Three woods in one sentence and not a tree among them: a surname, a set of clubs, then the same set again. The capital W is the only signpost on offer.
explanation.definitionFit: The first sense is the venue, the club as a place to play; 'woods' alone gives the clubs themselves, defining by naming one kind of them.

clue.text: Are you familiar with that woman delivered in Italian port?

indicators.note: A line is delivered when it is spoken out to an audience, so the question in front of the word is to be heard rather than read.

parts.words: Are you familiar with that woman
parts.note: the question collapses in speech to 'd'ye know 'er?', with the aitch dropped and the three words run together

explanation.walkthrough: The sounded phrase is a whole question rather than a single word, and it only works at conversational speed — the sort of run-together English nobody ever writes down.
explanation.definitionFit: Italian port → GENOA: the great harbour city on the north-west coast, birthplace of Columbus and still the country's busiest seaport.

clue.text: I'm seeking that special someone in foreign consulate, time and time again

definitions.note: The definition is a sentence spoken in the first person rather than a noun phrase: the setter lets the answer introduce itself, so read it as 'one who is seeking'.

indicators.note: What is foreign is out of its own country and out of place, so the letters beside the word have been moved from where they belong.

parts.note: nine letters of fodder, a country's office in a foreign city
T is the standard abbreviation for time, and the phrase asks for it twice over

explanation.walkthrough: 'Time and time again' reads as an idiom for endless repetition and is really an instruction to write one letter down twice. The definition speaks in the answer's own voice.
explanation.definitionFit: That is exactly a talent scout's job: touring clubs, gigs and auditions hunting for the one performer worth signing up.

clue.text: Mistakes rare at resorts

indicators.note: Read it as re-sorts: to sort a thing again is to put the very same items into a different order.

parts.note: six letters of fodder, which is the whole length of the entry

explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes a claim about holiday hotels, and the holiday word is the instruction. Watch for it: 'resorts' is a favourite because it hides a hyphen.
explanation.definitionFit: Mistakes → ERRATA: the Latin plural for errors, the slip of corrections a publisher tucks into a book once it has been printed.

clue.text: Extract of intro's transcribed as lecturers talk here

indicators.note: An extract is a passage lifted out of a longer text exactly as it stands, so the letters come out unshuffled and in the order they were in.

parts.note: six letters in a row, starting three into the first word and crossing both the apostrophe and the space

explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe is the only real obstacle, and it is not one: a hidden run ignores punctuation and the gaps between words and reads straight on through.
explanation.definitionFit: lecturers talk here → ROSTRA: rostra are the raised platforms a speaker stands on to address a hall, the Latin plural of rostrum.
